MAPThe workup, in order

LO 1Normal hematopoiesis

Q1. How does the family tree branch?
  • Hematopoietic stem cell (CD34+) →
    • Common myeloid progenitor → granulocytes, monocytes, RBCs, megakaryocytes/platelets
    • Common lymphoid progenitor → B cells (marrow), T cells (thymus), NK cells
  • Granulocytes: myeloblast → promyelocyte (primary/azurophilic granules) → myelocyte (secondary granules; last to divide) → metamyelocyte (kidney nucleus) → band → segmented neutrophil

Myelopoiesis

  • Stem cell → each myeloid line
Q2. Which growth factors drive each line?
FactorSourceDrives
EPOKidney (hypoxia)RBCs
TPOLiverMegakaryocytes → platelets
G-CSFMacrophages, stromaNeutrophils (filgrastim)
GM-CSF · M-CSFT cells, macrophagesGranulocytes + monocytes · monocytes
IL-3 · IL-5 · IL-7T cells · Th2 · stromaEarly progenitors · eosinophils · lymphoid
Stem cell factorStromaStem cells, mast cells (KIT)
Step 1

JAK2 sits under the EPO, TPO and G-CSF receptors → JAK2 V617F lets cells grow without the hormone (PV, ET, myelofibrosis).

Q3. What does a normal marrow and smear look like?
  • Niche: stroma (fibroblasts, adipocytes, osteoblasts, endothelium), matrix, sinusoids; needs iron, B12, folate
  • Site: adult = axial skeleton; fetus = yolk sac → liver/spleen → marrow
  • Cellularity ≈ 100 − age (≈50% fat at 50); M:E ≈ 3:1; large multinucleated megakaryocytes
  • A normal RBC is ≈ ⅔ the size of a small lymphocyte: use RBCs to call cells "small" vs "large"
  • Differential: neutrophils 50–70% > lymphocytes 20–40% > monocytes 2–8% > eosinophils 1–4% > basophils <1%

Normal marrow

  • ~50% cells, 50% fat (middle age)

Lymphocyte + neutrophil

  • RBC ≈ ⅔ the lymphocyte
Memory tool

Differential order: "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas." Cellularity: 100 − age.

Trap

Normal adult marrow does contain some lymphocytes (~10–15%). What's abnormal is a lymphoid aggregate (especially paratrabecular) or sheets of one cell type.

ApplyLO 1 application question

A1A 70-year-old's marrow is 90% cellular. Is that normal?
No: expected ≈30% (100 − 70). This is hypercellular.

LO 2WHO classification

Q1. How are WBC neoplasms grouped?
FamilyDefining ideaExamples
Myeloid neoplasms
Acute myeloid leukemia≥20% myeloblasts; maturation blockAML t(8;21), APL t(15;17)
MyelodysplasticIneffective, dysplastic; cytopenias; blasts <20%MDS del(5q); monosomy 5, 7
MyeloproliferativeEffective overproduction; tyrosine kinase mutationsCML (BCR-ABL), PV, ET, PMF (JAK2)
Lymphoid neoplasms
PrecursorLymphoblasts, TdT+B-ALL, T-ALL / lymphoblastic lymphoma
Mature BMimic a B-cell stageCLL/SLL, follicular, mantle, MZL, DLBCL, Burkitt, hairy cell, LPL, myeloma
Mature T/NKPost-thymic T cellsMycosis fungoides/Sézary, ATLL, ALCL
HodgkinFew RS cells, reactive backgroundClassic (4) and NLPHL

WHO = morphology + immunophenotype + genetics + clinical: ancillary studies are required.

Step 1 — the two-question sort

(1) Lineage: myeloid (MPO, CD13, CD33, CD117) vs lymphoid (B: CD19/20; T: CD3). (2) Maturity: blasts (TdT, CD34) vs mature cells.

In-house exam

Chromosome losses in MDS: monosomy 5 and 7.

Q2. What terms do I need?
TermMeaning
LymphadenopathyEnlarged node(s); nonspecific
Hyperplasia↑ cells; in nodes by pattern: follicular (B zone), paracortical (T zone; EBV, phenytoin), sinus histiocytosis
Auer rodPink-red needle in myeloid blast cytoplasm (fused primary granules); AML, especially APL
Russell bodyCytoplasmic PAS+ Ig; myeloma
Dutcher bodyIntranuclear Ig; Waldenström
Q3. How do I tell reactive hyperplasia from follicular lymphoma?
ReactiveFollicular lymphoma
FolliclesVaried sizes, in cortexCrowded, back-to-back, uniform, beyond capsule
Germinal centersPolarized, tingible-body macrophages, mitosesMonotonous, no polarity
MantleIntactThin/absent
BCL2 in GCNegativePositive
Clonalityκ and λLight-chain restricted

ApplyLO 2 application question

A1A 20-year-old with fever, sore throat and tender nodes has a node biopsy showing an expanded T zone with immunoblasts. Diagnosis?
Reactive paracortical hyperplasia (EBV / mono).

LO 3Leukemia vs lymphoma

Q1. How do leukemia and lymphoma differ?
LeukemiaLymphoma
OriginBone marrowLymph nodes, lymphoid tissue, solid organs
BloodSpill-over common; often high WBCUsually not
LineageMyeloid or lymphoidLymphoid only (HL vs NHL; B vs T)
TempoAcute (blasts) vs chronicIndolent vs aggressive
Presents asMarrow failure ± leukocytosisMass / lymphadenopathy
Memory tool

The name follows the location: same cells in marrow/blood = leukemia, in a node = lymphoma. Tumor cells in the blood → it's behaving as a leukemia.

Q2. Which diseases are both?
  • CLL ↔ SLL
  • ALL ↔ lymphoblastic lymphoma
  • Sézary ↔ mycosis fungoides
  • ATLL, Burkitt
  • Myeloid sarcoma = AML as a mass

CLL, hairy cell and mycosis fungoides are leukemias; follicular, mantle and marginal zone are lymphomas, not leukemias.

Trap — WBC count
  • High WBC ≠ leukemia: leukemoid reaction (left shift, high LAP, toxic granulation, Döhle bodies)
  • Leukemia ≠ high WBC: aleukemic leukemia; hairy cell → pancytopenia
  • Pancytopenia argues against an MPN

LO 4Signs and symptoms

Q1. How does the tumor's location produce symptoms?
Memory tool — marrow failure A-B-C

Anemia (fatigue) · Bleeding (platelets) · Contagion (neutrophils): "packed marrow, empty blood."

Step 1

Tender, rapidly enlarging node with fever → reactive. Painless, rubbery, progressive (>2 cm, supraclavicular, >4–6 weeks) → lymphoma → excisional biopsy.

Q2. How do the leukemias present?
Acute leukemiaCMLCLLHairy cell
OnsetAbruptInsidiousInsidiousIndolent, progressive
BloodHigh WBC (blasts) with neutropeniaVery high WBC, all stagesHigh WBC, mature lymphocytesPancytopenia, hairy cells
SymptomsBleeding, unusual (fungal) infectionsOrganomegalyDiffuse nodesSplenomegaly
CourseUrgent→ AML or fibrosisNot curableBRAF; long remissions
In-house exam

Hairy cell: circulating hairy cells, splenomegaly, pancytopenia.

LO 5Workup, ancillary tests and outcomes

Q1. What does each test answer?
TestAnswersClassic use
SmearWhat cells?Blasts, Auer rods, smudges, hairy cells, left shift, basophilia, rouleaux, dysplasia
ChemistryTurnover, organsLDH, uric acid (tumor lysis), Ca, creatinine, protein/albumin, β2-microglobulin
Marrow aspirateCell morphologyDifferential, flow, cytogenetics
Marrow coreArchitectureCellularity, fibrosis, infiltrates (paratrabecular aggregate)
Flow cytometryLineage, maturity, clonalityCLL (CD5/23), ALL (TdT), AML (CD13/33), hairy (CD103)
IHCMarkers in tissueBCL2 follicles, cyclin D1, CD15/30, CD138
CytochemistryMyeloid vs lymphoidMPO (AML), esterase (monocytic), TRAP (hairy), LAP (low in CML)
Cytogenetics / FISHTranslocationst(9;22), t(15;17), t(14;18), t(11;14), t(8;14), del(17p)
MolecularMutations, MRDBCR-ABL, JAK2, BRAF, MYD88, FLT3, NPM1
Protein studiesMonoclonal IgMyeloma, Waldenström, MGUS
High yield

Excisional node biopsy beats fine-needle aspiration: it shows the pattern (follicular vs diffuse, Hodgkin background) and gives enough tissue for ancillary tests.

Q2. How do I sort the small B-cell lymphomas?
LymphomaPatternCD5CD10CD23Cyclin D1Genetics
CLL/SLLDiffuse, proliferation centers+−+−Trisomy 12 (30%)
LymphoplasmacyticDiffuse−−−−MYD88; IgM
Mantle cellDiffuse, vaguely nodular+−−+t(11;14)
FollicularFollicular ± diffuse−+−/+−t(14;18) BCL2
Marginal zoneDiffuse, interfollicular−−+/−−Trisomy 18, t(11;18)
Memory tool — fast sort

CD5+? → CLL (CD23+) or mantle (cyclin D1+). CD10+? → follicular. Neither? → marginal zone or lymphoplasmacytic (IgM spike = LPL).

Q3. What are the expected outcomes?
DiseasePatientOutcome
ALLChild 2–10Kids ~90% cured; adults worse
AMLAdult ~65Remission 60–70%; transplant; APL excellent (ATRA)
CMLMiddle-agedNear-normal with TKIs; untreated → blast crisis
CLL · follicular · mantleOlderIndolent, incurable (4–10 y · 7–10 y · 3–5 y); → DLBCL
DLBCL · BurkittAdults · kidsAggressive but curable
Hairy cellOlder menLong remissions (cladribine)
HodgkinYoung + >5075–90% curable early; late effects
Myeloma~70Incurable

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A 5-year-old has fever, pallor, petechiae, leg pain and occasional blasts on smear. Next step?
Marrow aspirate + biopsy with flow cytometry and cytogenetics.
A2A 62-year-old with pneumonia has WBC 30k of mature neutrophils with Döhle bodies and high LAP. CML?
No: leukemoid reaction (CML has low LAP, basophilia, all stages, BCR-ABL).

LABSlide atlas

Method: (1) blood, marrow, node or organ? (2) cellularity / fat? (3) one cell type or a mix? (4) small vs large (compare with RBCs)? (5) special features: Auer rods, hairs, smudges, fibrosis, owl eyes, hof? (6) pattern: follicular, diffuse, paratrabecular?

Leukemias

ALL marrow

  • ~100% uniform blasts → cytopenias

AML smear

  • Big blasts, nucleoli, Auer rod

AML marrow

  • Packed blasts, one megakaryocyte, no fat

CML smear

  • Too many granulocytes, all stages

CML high power

  • Myelocytes, bands, basophils, eosinophils

CLL in liver

  • Portal tracts full of small lymphocytes

Hairy cell

  • Hair-like projections
In-house exam

AML smear = blasts + Auer rods (lumpy blasts with small purple rods). Bundles of Auer rods → APL.

Lymph nodes and non-Hodgkin lymphoma

Normal node

  • Capsule, sinus, follicles with germinal centers

Growth patterns

  • Follicular vs nodular vs diffuse

Lymphoma, gross

  • Fleshy tan nodes, little necrosis

Lymphoma in node

  • Through capsule into fat

DLBCL

  • Sheets of large cells, nucleoli

Paratrabecular aggregate

  • Hugging trabecula → follicular
In-house exam

Lymphoid aggregates hugging bony trabeculae → follicular lymphoma. Fleshy enlarged nodes → NHL. Large cells in sheets: lymphoma vs carcinoma → IHC (CD45/CD20 vs keratin).

Hodgkin lymphoma

Nodular sclerosis

  • Broad fibrous bands

Lymphocyte predominant

  • Sea of small lymphocytes; popcorn cells

Lymphocyte depleted

  • Many RS cells, few lymphocytes

Mixed cellularity

  • Mixed cells; CD15 lights RS cells

Reed-Sternberg cell

  • Binucleate, owl-eye nucleoli

Hodgkin in spleen

  • Pale nodules

Hodgkin in liver

  • White tumor spots (advanced stage)
High yield

Splenic masses are far more likely hematopoietic than metastatic carcinoma; >4 splenic nodules is an adverse factor in Hodgkin.

Plasma cell myeloma

Myeloma marrow

  • Sheets of near-normal plasma cells

Myeloma aspirate

  • Eccentric nuclei, hof, binucleate

Myeloma skull

  • Punched-out lucencies
In-house exam

Punched-out skull → myeloma; IL-6 (from plasma + stromal cells) drives plasma cell proliferation. Guaranteed question.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 3-year-old has 4 days of fever, gum bleeding and petechiae; WBC is 68,500/µL. What will the marrow show?

ALL: packed marrow, empty blood.

2An adult's smear shows large blasts with prominent nucleoli and pink needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions. These inclusions are:

AML, especially APL.

3What is the expected marrow cellularity of a healthy 60-year-old?

100 − age.

4Which growth factor is made by the liver and drives platelet production?

EPO = kidney.

5A marrow core shows a lymphoid aggregate lining a bony trabecula beside normal myeloid cells. Most likely diagnosis?

Paratrabecular = follicular; benign aggregates are central.

6A 58-year-old has a painless 3-cm supraclavicular node for 2 months. Best biopsy?

Architecture + tissue for ancillary tests.

7A 66-year-old's node shows small B cells that are CD5+, CD23−, CD10−. Which confirms the diagnosis?

Mantle cell lymphoma.

8A 62-year-old with pneumonia has WBC 30,000/µL of mature neutrophils, toxic granulation, Döhle bodies and high LAP. Diagnosis?

CML has low LAP and basophilia.

9Which pair is the same disease presenting as a leukemia or a lymphoma?

Also ALL/lymphoblastic lymphoma, Sézary/MF.

10Which cytokine drives plasma cell proliferation in myeloma?

From plasma cells and stroma.

11Pancytopenia argues against which diagnosis?

MPNs raise counts.

12A tissue mass shows sheets of large cells. Which IHC pair best separates lymphoma from carcinoma?

Lymphoma = CD45/CD20; carcinoma = keratin.
